title: One Layer Versus the Whole Band
takeaway: Repeating the word-list capacity measurement at a single workspace layer instead of pooling over the whole band leaves the qualitative picture unchanged, but cuts the counts sharply: on lists of unrelated words, roughly six items are present at a time when any layer may supply the evidence, against one or two at layer 79 alone. The paper reads the gap as a sign that the workspace stores different concepts in different layers, which raises its effective capacity.
walkthrough:
The item is a four-panel comparison in two rows. Both rows run the same measurement. They differ only in how many layers the measurement is allowed to consult.

The measurement is the [[word-list-experiment]]. The model reads a comma-separated list of 80 words. At every comma the [[j-lens-readout]] scores and ranks every vocabulary token, and a list word counts as present if its rank is 25 or better.

The top row reproduces panels B and C of the main list figure without change. Presence there is decided by band-min. The word's rank is computed separately at each layer of the [[workspace-layers]] band — L38 through L92 in the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] convention — and the smallest of those ranks, the best one, is the one compared against the threshold. A word therefore counts as present if it clears the bar anywhere in the band.

The bottom row repeats both panels at one layer, L79. Rank comes from that layer alone. A word held at L60 and nowhere else no longer counts.

### Reading the panels

Panel B, in either row, plots the number of list words present against comma position. Orange traces single-family lists, pooled over four families; blue traces lists of unrelated words. Solid lines count only words already read; dashed lines count all 80. Shading is the interquartile range. Panel C varies the rank threshold $K$ and reports how many already-read words clear it near the end of the list, with grey control words that never appear in the prompt setting the chance level.

### What the comparison shows

The shape survives. Words from a related family persist in the readout longer than words from a random list, and the dashed orange line still climbs to nearly the whole family within the first few items, unread members included. [[category-loading]] is not an artifact of pooling layers.

The scale does not survive. On random lists the band-min row shows about six read words present at once; the single-layer row shows one or two.

The paper takes that difference as evidence that the [[j-space]] can park distinct concepts at distinct depths, so [[j-space-capacity]] measured across the band exceeds capacity at any one layer. The argument is an inference from two counts, not a direct reading of which layer holds which word ([[single-layer-capacity]]).

terms.definition: The presence rule used in the top row: a word's J-lens rank is computed at every layer of the workspace band and the minimum, meaning the best, is kept. Presence anywhere in the band counts as presence.

The presence rule used in the bottom row: rank is read at layer 79 only, so a word represented at some other workspace layer does not count. Layer 79 is the same late workspace layer used for the example readouts in the main list figure.
The workspace layer range, given in the paper's percentage indexing. The J-space is near empty below L38 and turns into output-driving content above L92.
The paper samples 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers and relabels them 0 to 100, so a layer number reads as a percentage of the model's depth rather than as an index into its stack.

The read operation whose ranking decides presence: the residual stream at a layer is passed through the Jacobian lens to give a score for every vocabulary token, and the tokens are sorted by that score.

The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors, which the paper argues serves the model as a workspace. This figure asks how much of it is visible at one depth versus across the band.
A word's position in the readout's ordering over the whole vocabulary. Lower is better, so the best rank over a set of layers is the smallest one.
The cutoff for counting a list word as present in the readout. It is fixed at 25 in panel B and swept in panel C.
Number of list words present in the readout at each comma of the list, for single-family lists against unrelated lists. The top row uses band-min presence, the bottom row single-layer presence.
The threshold sweep: how many already-read words fall at rank K or better near the end of the list, as K varies. It checks that the findings do not rest on the choice of 25.
80-word lists drawn from a single category, with results pooled over four families. These load the readout as a whole category within a few items.
80-word lists of items with no shared category, drawn at random. These are where the band-min and single-layer counts diverge most.
In panel B, the count restricted to list words the model has already read at that comma.
In panel B, the count over all 80 list words, including those not yet read. Its rise on family lists is the signature of category loading.
The band around each curve, giving the interquartile range over trials.
Words that never appear in the prompt, counted the same way as list words. They set the chance level for the threshold sweep.
The rank cutoff swept along panel C's horizontal axis. Everywhere else in the figure it is held at 25.

How many distinct concepts the workspace can hold at once in practice. The paper's claim here is that the figure it takes across the band is larger than the figure at any single layer, because layers can hold different things.

numbers.meaning: The workspace band over which the top row takes its minimum rank. These are the two depths at which the paper's boundary metrics inflect: below L38 the J-space carries almost nothing, above L92 its content turns into the imminent output.

The single layer used in the bottom row, about 79% of the way through the model. It sits late in the workspace band and is the layer the main list figure already used for its example readouts, which makes the two rows directly comparable.
Words per list. The length matters here because it is far above every count reported, so neither row is limited by running out of list.
The rank threshold for presence. A word must reach the readout's top 25 vocabulary tokens to be counted, at any band layer in the top row or at L79 in the bottom row.
Read words from a random list present at a given comma under band-min presence. This is the count carried over from the main list figure and is the number the single-layer row is set against.

The same count at L79 alone. Requiring one layer to hold the word, rather than accepting any layer in the band, removes roughly three quarters of the items. The gap is what the paper reads as concepts being distributed across depth.
The number of word families pooled into the orange curves of panel B, carried over unchanged from the main list figure.
The layout: two panels, B and C, shown twice - once with band-min presence on top and once with single-layer presence below. Only the presence rule changes between rows.
The range of the paper's layer numbering. 25 evenly spaced layers are relabeled as percentages of depth, which is why L38, L79 and L92 read as fractions rather than as layer indices.
